title: A magazine cover
text: The magazine cover [show|shows|'The cover' is singular, so add -s.] a young woman in the foreground. She is wearing [a expensive|an expensive|Use 'an' before a vowel sound.] dress, which suggests that she is wealthy. The bright [colour|colours|There are several colours here, so use the plural.] create a happy mood. The target audience is probably young [woman|women|More than one person, so use the plural 'women'.].

title: A sports advert
text: The advert represents the man as [strongly|strong|After 'represent someone as', use an adjective.] and successful. The camera angle makes him [looks|look|After 'make someone', use the base verb.] powerful. This [reinforce|reinforces|'This' is singular, so add -s.] the stereotype that men should be strong. There [is|are|'There are' + a plural noun.] no women in the image, so it is not a realistic representation.

title: A news photograph
text: The photo was [take|taken|Passive: was + past participle 'taken'.] in a hospital. The nurse's facial expression is [care|caring|You need an adjective here: caring.]. In the background, there are many [patient|patients|After 'many', use a plural noun.]. The headline describes her as a hero, which creates [an positive|a positive|Use 'a' before a consonant sound.] representation of nurses.

title: A charity poster
text: The purpose [for|of|We say 'the purpose of' something.] the poster is to make people recycle. It uses a close-up of a turtle, which looks [vulnerability|vulnerable|After 'looks', you need an adjective.]. The dark lighting [create|creates|'The lighting' is singular, so add -s.] a serious mood. The poster has a strong effect [to|on|We say 'an effect on' someone.] the audience.

title: Two family adverts
text: The first advert represents the family as [tradition|traditional|You need an adjective: traditional.]. The mother [is cook|is cooking|Present continuous: is + -ing.] in the kitchen, and the father [read|reads|'The father' is singular, so add -s.] a newspaper. This is a stereotypical image. The second advert [challenge|challenges|'The second advert' is singular, so add -s.] this idea because the father is cooking.

title: A perfume advert
text: The setting is [an luxury|a luxury|Use 'a' before a consonant sound.] hotel. The model is young and [attraction|attractive|You need an adjective here: attractive.]. text: The headline describes the team as [success|successful|After 'describe someone as', use an adjective.]. text: A social media post [show|shows|'A social media post' is singular, so add -s.] a father making breakfast for his two [childs|children|The plural of 'child' is 'children'.]. title: Supermarket coffee
text: A sponsored social post shows a supermarket cashier taking a coffee break with a colleague. They sit outside the store in [ordinery|ordinary|Spell 'ordinary' with -ary.] uniforms, sharing biscuits from a paper bag. The post has no celebrity or perfect kitchen. [It's|Its|'It's' means 'it is'. 'Its' shows belonging: its caption.] caption says, “Good coffee for the days that start early.” The packet and price are shown [clear|clearly|Use the adverb 'clearly' to say how they are shown.], followed by a link to the supermarket.

title: Speciality coffee
text: During a podcast, the host describes visiting a coffee grower and watching the beans being [sort|sorted|After 'being', use the past participle: sorted.]. We hear birds and people talking behind her voice. She says the speciality coffee has a bright taste and [explain|explains|'She' takes a verb with -s: explains.] how she makes it at home. The [growers|grower’s|Add ’s to show that the name belongs to the grower.] name and the brand’s website are read aloud at the end, along with the price of a trial bag.

title: Sports drink
text: A radio advert begins with the sounds of a school running club. Trainers [hits|hit|'Trainers' is plural, so use 'hit'.] the track, and several young people cheer each other on. One girl stops for a drink before going back to [helping|help|After 'to', use the base verb: to help.] a friend finish. The narrator says the sports drink is “for every kind of finish.” A shop name and the price of a bottle [closes|close|'A shop name and the price' is plural, so use 'close'.] the advert.

title: Bottled water
text: Before a cinema film, a bottled-water advert follows a night worker leaving a hospital as the sun [raises|rises|'Raise' needs an object. The sun 'rises' by itself.]. She drinks from a bottle while waiting for a bus and smiles when her son [send|sends|'Her son' is one person, so add -s.] her a message. There is [few|little|Use 'little' with uncountable nouns like dialogue.] dialogue. The music grows warmer as the bus arrives, and the final screen shows the bottle with the words “Take care of your day.”

title: Everyday watch
text: A sponsored post shows an everyday watch on the [wrist's|wrists|This is a plural, not belonging, so it has no apostrophe: wrists.] of three people. A chef checks it before [open|opening|After 'before', use the -ing form: before opening.] a café, a parent checks it outside a school, and a teenager checks it before a bus arrives. Each [are|is|'Each' takes a singular verb: each is shown.] shown doing an ordinary task. The caption reads, “Time for the things you do.” The [watches|watch’s|Add ’s to show that the price belongs to the watch.] price and three strap colours appear below.

title: Luxury watch
text: A magazine advert shows a woman in a tailored suit standing alone in [a|an|Use 'an' before a vowel sound: an empty concert hall.] empty concert hall. She checks a luxury watch before [step|stepping|After 'before', use the -ing form: before stepping.] onto the stage to conduct an orchestra. The audience has not arrived yet. Gold light [fall|falls|'Gold light' is singular, so add -s.] on the watch, while her face stays partly in shadow. The line “Before they see you” appears above the brand name, with no price.

title: School trainers
text: Before a cinema film, an advert follows two children walking to school in the same style of trainers. One child runs ahead, while the other moves more [slow|slowly|Use the adverb 'slowly' to say how the child moves.] with a walking aid. They meet at the school gate and compare the [colour's|colours|This is a plural, not belonging, so it has no apostrophe: colours.] of their shoes. The line “Different mornings. Same way in” appears beside the trainers, their price and the shop name.

title: Designer trainers
text: A podcast host describes watching a street dancer practise for a performance. She says the dancer [weared|wore|The past of 'wear' is 'wore'.] designer trainers and kept [repeat|repeating|After 'kept', use the -ing form: kept repeating.] a [dificult|difficult|Spell 'difficult' with a double f.] step after everyone else had left. A short recording of the music plays beneath the story. The host then names the designer and gives the date when the limited shoes [becomes|become|'The limited shoes' is plural, so use 'become'.] available. The price is mentioned at the end.

title: Waterproof coat
text: In an online video, a father and daughter walk to school [threw|through|'Threw' is the past of 'throw'. 'Through' means from one side to the other.] heavy rain. The daughter wears a waterproof coat, but the father has only an umbrella that [keep|keeps|'An umbrella' is singular, so add -s.] turning inside out. They laugh when she offers [he|him|After 'offers', use 'him'.] her hood. At the gate, she takes off the coat and shows that her uniform is dry. The video ends with three sizes and a clear price.

title: Designer coat
text: A billboard shows a designer coat [hang|hanging|After 'shows a designer coat', use the -ing form: hanging.] on the back of a chair in an empty theatre. Beyond it, an actor stands on stage during a rehearsal. The [coats|coat’s|Add ’s to show that the lining belongs to the coat.] red lining is the only strong colour in the picture. The words “An entrance worth making” sit beside the brand name. There [are|is|'There is' goes with a singular noun: no model.] no model wearing it and no price on the billboard.

title: Basic handbag
text: A magazine page shows a care worker carrying a basic handbag on a bus. Inside [is|are|Four things are listed, so use 'are'.] a lunch box, house keys, a notebook and a small gift for someone she [visit|visits|'She' takes a verb with -s: visits.]. The advert uses four close pictures to show each [pockets|pocket|After 'each', use a singular noun: pocket.]. Its main line says, “Room for the whole day.” The bag is shown in two colours, with the price printed [clear|clearly|Use the adverb 'clearly' to say how the price is printed.] underneath.

title: Designer handbag
text: A double-page magazine advert for a designer handbag shows an [elder|older|'Elder' is used for family members, as in 'my elder sister'. For age in general, use 'older'.] woman and her adult daughter standing in a lift. They each [carries|carry|After 'they each', the verb agrees with 'they': carry.] the same style in a different colour. The daughter smiles at the mirror, while the mother looks towards the open door. The line “Never just one story” appears across the pages. The bags and brand name [is|are|'The bags and brand name' is plural, so use 'are'.] shown without prices.

title: Everyday fragrance
text: A social media video shows a teenage boy getting ready for his first day at a new college. He puts on an everyday fragrance, then stops at the door and [check|checks|'He' takes a verb with -s: checks.] his timetable again. A classmate later invites him to [sitting|sit|After 'invite someone to', use the base verb: sit.] with a group. The caption says, “Feel ready for the first hello.” The bottle and an [affordible|affordable|Spell 'affordable' with -able.] price appear beside a shop link.

title: Luxury perfume
text: A sponsored post for a luxury perfume shows a woman getting ready for an awards dinner. She [take|takes|'She' takes a verb with -s: takes.] off her jewellery, changes into a [plane|plain|A 'plane' flies. Simple, with no pattern, is 'plain'.] black dress and adds the perfume last. The camera stays [closely|close|After 'stays', use an adjective: close.] to her hands rather than showing the other guests. The caption reads, “What remains when everything else is quiet.” The bottle appears on a dark background with no price.

title: Budget smartphone
text: In a radio advert, a man explains that he [need|needs|'He' takes a verb with -s: needs.] a phone for calls, messages and taking pictures of his [grandchildrens|grandchildren|'Grandchildren' is already plural.]. We hear him ask a shop worker [weather|whether|'Weather' is rain and sun. 'Whether' introduces a choice.] the budget smartphone can do those things. She answers each question [plain|plainly|Use the adverb 'plainly' to say how she answers.] and gives the price. At the end, his granddaughter laughs at the first photo he sends her, and the brand name is repeated.

title: Flagship smartphone
text: A television advert shows a woman recording a street musician at night on a flagship smartphone. She [send|sends|'She' takes a verb with -s: sends.] the video to her brother, [which|who|Use 'who' for a person.] is watching from another city. The camera cuts between her bright screen and his dark living room. A voiceover says, “Bring them closer to what you see.” The phone appears in several colours, while the price is [leaved|left|The past participle of 'leave' is 'left'.] off screen.

title: Language-learning app
text: A banner on a travel website shows a woman arriving at a small [restaurent|restaurant|Spell 'restaurant' with -ant.] in another country. Her phone [display|displays|'Her phone' is singular, so add -s.] a short lesson from a language app, and she orders her meal using a new phrase. The server answers and she smiles, then asks [he|him|After 'asks', use 'him'.] to repeat the last word. A green “Try a free lesson” button appears below the app logo.

title: Gaming headphones
text: A radio advert begins with two friends speaking during an online game. One cannot hear the other over the [noize|noise|Spell 'noise' with an s.] from his room, so he [put|puts|'He' takes a verb with -s: puts.] on gaming headphones and asks her to say the plan again. We hear her voice clearly this time. The narrator [name|names|'The narrator' is one person, so add -s.] the microphone feature and gives the price, followed by a short line from the friends celebrating together.

title: Premium noise-cancelling headphones
text: A television advert follows a man commuting across a [noisey|noisy|Spell 'noisy' without an e.] city. On the train, he puts on premium noise-cancelling headphones, and the traffic sound fades. He can still [hears|hear|After 'can', use the base verb: hear.] an announcement when he chooses a different setting. The final shot shows him arriving at a rehearsal with his violin. The voiceover says, “Choose what gets through,” and the product name appears.

title: Family tablet
text: A television advert shows a family tablet being [use|used|After 'being', use the past participle: used.] at three different times. In the morning, a child reads a story. Later, his sister draws a map, and their grandmother joins a video call in the evening. Each person [open|opens|'Each person' takes a singular verb: opens.] a separate profile. The closing screen shows the tablet beside the words “A place for everyone,” with [it's|its|'It's' means 'it is'. 'Its' shows belonging: its storage size.] storage size and price below.

title: Professional camera
text: A podcast host describes photographing a school play with a professional camera. She could not move close to the stage, but she says the faces [was|were|'The faces' is plural, so use 'were'.] still clear in her pictures. We hear the curtain open and the audience clap. She names the lens she [use|used|She used it in the past, so use 'used'.] and explains that the camera can be [test|tested|After 'can be', use the past participle: tested.] at a local shop. The price is available online.

title: Fitness tracker
text: An online video shows a fitness tracker on the wrist of a woman who [work|works|'Who' refers to one woman, so use 'works'.] at a desk. When it [remembers|reminds|You 'remember' something yourself. To make someone else remember is to 'remind' them.] her to move, she walks downstairs and meets a neighbour outside. Later, they begin taking short walks together. The screen shows steps rather than [wait|weight|To 'wait' is to stay until something happens. How heavy you are is your 'weight'.]. At the end, a line reads, “A little movement can lead somewhere,” next to the tracker’s price.

title: Home security system
text: A radio advert begins with a doorbell while a family is away. A home security camera [send|sends|'A home security camera' is singular, so add -s.] an alert to the [mothers|mother’s|Add ’s to show that the phone belongs to the mother.] phone, and she sees a delivery driver leaving a parcel. She tells her partner that it has [arrive|arrived|After 'has', use the past participle: arrived.]. The narrator explains the camera and monthly service fee, then says the family can check the door from anywhere with a connection.

title: Entry-level laptop
text: A website banner shows an entry-level laptop at a kitchen table. A father uses it to [applying|apply|After 'to', use the base verb: to apply.] for a job, while his daughter waits to finish her school project. The two screens [appears|appear|'The two screens' is plural, so use 'appear'.] side by side to show that the laptop can handle both [task|tasks|After 'both', use a plural noun: tasks.]. The price is large and a blue button says, “See what it can do.”

title: Family car
text: A television advert shows a family car outside a [swiming|swimming|Double the m: swimming.] pool. Two fathers [loads|load|'Two fathers' is plural, so use 'load'.] towels and bags into the boot while their children argue about who [winned|won|The past of 'win' is 'won'.] the race. The children climb in, still wearing wet hair. The voiceover says, “There’s room for the whole story.” The final shot shows the number of seats, the price and the car in three colours.

title: Luxury car
text: In a podcast advert, the host describes being [drove|driven|After 'being', use the past participle: driven.] to a meeting in a luxury car. She remembers the quiet inside, even when the road outside [were|was|'The road' is singular, so use 'was'.] crowded. Her guest asks whether the car made her [fewer|less|Use 'less' with adjectives: less nervous.] nervous. She laughs and says it gave her time to prepare. The brand name follows, with an invitation to arrange a private test drive.

title: City bicycle
text: A poster in a station shows a woman cycling to work in ordinary [cloths|clothes|'Cloths' are pieces of material for cleaning. Things you wear are 'clothes'.]. She stops at a crossing beside people walking and [take|takes|'She' takes a verb with -s: takes.] a [fold|folded|Use 'folded' to describe the jacket.] jacket from her basket. The city bicycle is shown from the side, with a map of nearby cycle paths underneath. The line “The short way across town” appears above a price and a shop address.

title: Racing bicycle
text: A racing bicycle billboard shows a rider reaching the top of a hill at dawn. Another rider, [more|much|Use 'much' before a comparative: much older.] older, is close behind her. Both are shown working [hardly|hard|'Hardly' means 'almost not'. Here we need 'hard'.], and neither appears to be winning. The frame and wheels are lit clearly. The words “Keep finding another climb” appear beside a team logo, but the price is not shown.

title: Budget hotel stay
text: A poster inside a train shows three friends checking into a budget hotel after a concert. One [carry|carries|'One' is singular, so use 'carries'.] a guitar case and another has [fell|fallen|After 'has', use the past participle: fallen.] asleep on her feet. They see the room price on a screen at reception and laugh with [releif|relief|I before e except after c: relief.]. The poster says, “A bed when the music ends,” followed by a map showing the hotel near the station.

title: Luxury hotel stay
text: A podcast host describes a luxury hotel where a worker noticed her mother found stairs difficult. The worker showed them a room close to the lift without being [ask|asked|After 'being', use the past participle: asked.]. The host speaks about the sea view [to|too|'Too' means 'as well' here.], but returns to that small act of care. Soft music plays before the hotel name and a booking address [is|are|'The hotel name and a booking address' is plural, so use 'are'.] read aloud.

title: Household vacuum cleaner
text: An online video for a household vacuum cleaner shows a family tidying up after a birthday party. The teenage son [begin|begins|'The teenage son' is one person, so add -s.] the cleaning while his father takes down decorations. A close shot follows [crumb's|crumbs|This is a plural, not belonging, so it has no apostrophe: crumbs.] disappearing from under a table. The child who had the birthday [fall|falls|'The child' is singular, so add -s.] asleep on the sofa. The last screen gives the price and the words “Ready for tomorrow.”

title: Premium robot vacuum
text: Before a cinema film, a premium robot vacuum moves through a busy home. A woman watches it turn around her [fathers|father’s|Add ’s to show that the walking stick belongs to her father.] walking stick rather than bumping into it. Later, he moves the chair so it can [cleans|clean|After 'can', use the base verb: clean.] underneath. The camera follows both people as they [makes|make|'They' is plural, so use 'make'.] space for the machine. The advert ends with the app controls and a premium price.

title: Flat-pack sofa
text: A banner on a furniture website shows three flat-pack sofa boxes arriving at a small apartment. A woman and her brother [builds|build|'A woman and her brother' is plural, so use 'build'.] the sofa together, following pictures on a sheet. The next image shows them sitting on it with [there|their|'There' is a place. 'Their' shows belonging: their dog.] dog between them. The words “Your place, your hands” [appears|appear|'The words' is plural, so use 'appear'.] next to the price and an assembly video button.

title: Designer sofa
text: A designer sofa billboard shows a grandmother sitting with her grandson on a long green sofa. He is [learning|teaching|The student is 'learning'. The person giving the lesson is 'teaching'.] her a card game, and the cards are [spreaded|spread|The past participle of 'spread' is 'spread'.] between them. The room is simple, with a large window and almost no other [furnitures|furniture|'Furniture' is uncountable, so it has no plural.]. The line “Space for what matters” appears in small letters beside the brand name. There [are|is|'There is' goes with a singular noun: no price.] no price.

title: Shampoo
text: A magazine advert for shampoo shows a woman after swimming practice. She wears a team jacket and [carry|carries|'She' takes a verb with -s: carries.] a bag with wet [towles|towels|Spell 'towels' with -els.]. In the second picture, she washes her hair at home before [join|joining|After 'before', use the -ing form: before joining.] friends for dinner. The bottle stands between the images. The words “From one part of your day to the next” appear beside a clear shop price.

title: Premium skincare serum
text: A website banner for premium skincare serum shows a woman in her [sixty's|sixties|No apostrophe is needed: her sixties.] looking directly at the camera. The photograph leaves the lines on her face [visibly|visible|After 'leaves the lines', use the adjective: visible.]. Beside it, a close shot shows her using a small [number|amount|Use 'amount' with uncountable things like serum.] of serum. The line “Care that begins with your skin” sits above an ingredients link and a button to see the price.

title: Mobile data plan
text: Before a cinema film, a mobile data plan advert follows a son sending short [video's|videos|This is a plural, not belonging, so it has no apostrophe: videos.] to his mother while travelling. She watches him cross a bridge, then [replys|replies|Change y to -ies: replies.] with a video of the family dog at home. The voiceover says, “Keep sharing the small things.” The monthly price and data limit [appears|appear|'The monthly price and data limit' is plural, so use 'appear'.] on screen long enough to read.

title: Private tutoring service
text: In an online video, a private tutor meets a student who can explain an idea aloud but [struggle|struggles|'Who' refers to one student, so use 'struggles'.] to write it down. She listens first, then asks him to turn one sentence into a paragraph. He reads it back to her with a smile. The advert gives the [tutors|tutor’s|Add ’s to show that the experience belongs to the tutor.] experience and lesson price at the end, [following|followed|We say 'followed by' something.] by a booking link.

title: Gym membership
text: A gym membership billboard shows a woman in work clothes standing beside a weight machine. A trainer [explain|explains|'A trainer' is one person, so add -s.] how to set it, and a second photograph shows her [try|trying|After 'shows her', use the -ing form: trying.] it herself. Other members look [busily|busy|After 'look', use an adjective: busy.] with their own exercises. The line “Nobody starts as an expert” sits above the monthly fee and the gym’s opening hours.

title: Wellness retreat
text: A poster inside a train shows a woman arriving at a wellness retreat with a suitcase and a work laptop. In the next picture, the laptop is [close|closed|Use 'closed' here: the laptop is shut.] while she [join|joins|'She' takes a verb with -s: joins.] a group walk. The line “Leave room for yourself” appears above the [retreats|retreat’s|Add ’s to show that the dates belong to the retreat.] dates. The poster also lists the cost of the three-day stay in small print.

title: Children’s board game
text: In a radio advert for a children’s board game, we hear a child reading a card aloud. Her uncle chooses the wrong answer and everyone [laugh|laughs|'Everyone' takes a singular verb: laughs.]. A voice explains that players work in teams, then gives the game’s age range and price. The sound of the final card being turned [close|closes|The verb goes with 'the sound', not 'card', so use 'closes'.] the advert before the brand name.

title: Collectable toy set
text: A television advert shows a collectable toy set on a shelf in a teenager’s room. She [careful|carefully|Use the adverb 'carefully' to say how she opens it.] opens a new figure, reads its numbered card and places it next to older ones. Her younger brother asks why she keeps the [boxs|boxes|Add -es after x: boxes.]. She explains which picture [belong|belongs|'Which picture' is singular, so add -s.] to each figure. The advert ends with the release date and a shop list.

title: Streaming subscription
text: A poster on a station platform shows a father and daughter choosing different programmes on a streaming service. He [watch|watches|'He' takes a verb with -s: watches.] a cooking show on his phone, while she watches a cartoon on a tablet. They put the screens away when their train [arrive|arrives|'Their train' is singular, so add -s.]. The monthly price and number of available profiles are [print|printed|After 'are', use the past participle: printed.] below the words “Your journey, your choice.”

title: Premium bank account
text: An online video for a premium bank account follows a business owner arriving [lately|late|'Lately' means 'recently'. Not on time is 'late'.] at an airport. She calls the [accounts|account’s|Add ’s to show that the service belongs to the account.] travel support service and [get|gets|'She' takes a verb with -s: gets.] help changing her booking. The advert shows the call rather than a luxury lounge. The final screen lists the monthly fee and travel benefit, with a link to the full account terms.

title: Orange juice
text: A poster inside a train shows a young delivery worker drinking orange juice while he [wait|waits|'He' takes a verb with -s: waits.] for the first service of the morning. His bicycle is beside him, and his phone displays several [adresses|addresses|Spell 'addresses' with a double d and a double s.]. Across the poster, the words “A fresh start for every shift” appear in orange. The carton and a low price are printed near the route map. Other passengers are [blurring|blurred|The photographer has blurred them, so use 'are blurred'.] behind him, so the worker and the drink [is|are|'The worker and the drink' is plural, so use 'are'.] the first things commuters notice.

title: Cold-pressed juice
text: On another train platform, a cold-pressed juice poster shows a woman in running clothes beside a man wearing office clothes. They each hold the same glass bottle, but stand at opposite ends of the image. The label names the fruit and the date the juice was [make|made|After 'was', use the past participle: made.]. A narrow line of text reads, “However your day begins.” The price is [absence|absent|After 'is', use the adjective: absent.], and the platform’s grey walls [makes|make|'The platform's grey walls' is plural, so use 'make'.] the green bottles look [especialy|especially|Spell 'especially' with -lly: especial + ly.] bright.

title: Breakfast cereal
text: A breakfast cereal billboard shows a mother leaving home for a night shift as her partner [prepare|prepares|'Her partner' is one person, so add -s.] breakfast for their son. She takes a small bowl with her while the boy sits at the table. Both adults wear work clothes, and nobody [speak|speaks|'Nobody' takes a singular verb: speaks.] in the photograph. The tagline reads, “Morning happens at different times.” A large cereal box [fill|fills|'A large cereal box' is singular, so add -s.] the right-hand side, with a supermarket price printed below the family.

title: Boxed chocolates
text: Before a cinema screening, a boxed-chocolate advert shows a father visiting his adult daughter in a new apartment. He has wrapped the chocolates [hisself|himself|There is no word 'hisself'. Use 'himself'.], but the ribbon is uneven. She opens the box, [recognise|recognises|'She' takes a verb with -s: recognises.] the brand and offers him the first piece. The camera pauses on [there|their|'There' is a place. 'Their' shows belonging: their hands.] hands rather than their faces. Soft music plays as the words “For the moments you make” [appears|appear|'The words' is plural, so use 'appear'.] beside the product and an online shop address.

title: Instant noodles
text: A podcast host describes an instant-noodle dinner she shared with her younger brother after helping him [moving|move|After 'help someone', use the base verb: move.] into a student room. He had no plates, so they [eat|ate|The story is in the past, so use 'ate'.] from the bowls in the kitchen box. We hear the kettle click and the two of them laughing. She reads the packet’s price and preparation time, then names the supermarket where it is [sell|sold|After 'is', use the past participle: sold.]. The story presents a cheap meal as part of a new [begining|beginning|Double the n: beginning.].

title: Meal kit
text: In a radio advert for a meal kit, a woman tells her partner she wants to cook for friends but has never [make|made|After 'has never', use the past participle: made.] the dish on the menu. We hear vegetables being [chopping|chopped|After 'being', use the past participle: chopped.] while the kit’s recipe is read aloud between their jokes. The friends arrive just as the oven sounds. A narrator explains what [come|comes|'What' takes a singular verb here: what comes.] in each box, states the price for two or four people and gives a website for choosing next [weeks|week’s|Add ’s to show that the meals belong to next week.] meals.

title: Supermarket coffee
text: A sponsored social post for supermarket coffee shows four workers finishing different late shifts. A cleaner, a driver, a nurse and a shop worker each [makes|make|The subject is four workers, so use 'make'.] a cup at home before they sleep. The pictures use warm kitchen light but leave their uniforms [visibly|visible|After 'leave their uniforms', use the adjective: visible.]. The caption reads, “For every kind of morning,” followed by the packet price. Comments from customers [describes|describe|'Comments' is plural, so use 'describe'.] when they drink it, and the supermarket replies with [it's|its|'It's' means 'it is'. 'Its' shows belonging: its opening times.] opening times.

title: Speciality coffee
text: A speciality-coffee billboard outside an office building shows a grower standing among coffee plants, holding a small bag with his name on it. Beside him, a barista in the city serves a cup made from those beans. A thin line [connect|connects|'A thin line' is singular, so add -s.] the two photographs. The copy reads, “Know where your morning begins.” The [cafes|café’s|Add ’s to show that the address belongs to the café.] address appears clearly, while the price is printed [more|much|Use 'much' before a comparative: much smaller.] smaller near the bottom.

title: Sports drink
text: A magazine advert for a sports drink shows a teenage wheelchair basketball player practising after her teammates [has|have|'Her teammates' is plural, so use 'have'.] left. A coach [pass|passes|'A coach' is one person, so add -s.] her the ball, and she takes another shot. The bottle stands on the floor beside her chair, within reach. The headline says, “The work nobody sees.” The drink’s ingredients and price [appears|appear|'The ingredients and price' is plural, so use 'appear'.] in a small panel, while the full-page photograph gives most of its space to her [concentrate|concentration|After 'her', use a noun: concentration.].

title: Bottled water
text: An online video for bottled water follows a grandfather teaching his grandson how to [planting|plant|After 'how to', use the base verb: plant.] vegetables. They take a [brake|break|A 'brake' stops a car. A rest is a 'break'.] in the shade and share water from two bottles. The boy asks why they must [waits|wait|After 'must', use the base verb: wait.] for the seeds to grow, and the grandfather laughs. The voiceover says, “Good things take time.” The bottles appear on a garden table, and the final screen [list|lists|'The final screen' is singular, so add -s.] the price and shops selling them.

title: Everyday watch
text: An online advert for an everyday watch shows a woman who [manage|manages|'Who' refers to one woman, so use 'manages'.] the morning school run with her sister. One prepares breakfast while the other takes the children to the bus stop. They check [identicle|identical|Spell 'identical' with -al.] watches as they pass keys [among|between|Use 'between' for two people.] them. The video uses quick cuts but no dramatic music. The final line reads, “Made for days you share,” followed by a large price, a warranty line and three available strap colours.

title: Luxury watch
text: A luxury-watch billboard shows an older architect alone in her studio at night. Models of buildings [surrounds|surround|'Models of buildings' is plural, so use 'surround'.] her, and the city beyond the window is dark. She turns a watch in her hands before [put|putting|After 'before', use the -ing form: before putting.] it on. A narrow beam of light catches [it's|its|'It's' means 'it is'. 'Its' shows belonging: its face.] face. The words “Time leaves a mark” sit under the brand name. Nothing on the board [identify|identifies|'Nothing' takes a singular verb: identifies.] a price or explains whether the watch is connected to her work.

title: School trainers
text: A radio advert for school trainers begins with a child asking her father whether she can walk to school [by|on|We say 'on her own' or 'by herself'.] her own. We hear the front door close and her shoes move along different streets. She meets a friend at the crossing and they arrive together. The [fathers|father’s|Add ’s to show that the voice belongs to the father.] voice says she is growing up [quick|quickly|Use the adverb 'quickly' to say how she is growing up.]. The narrator names the trainers, [mention|mentions|'The narrator' is one person, so add -s.] their strong straps and gives a price available in several shops.

title: Designer trainers
text: A designer-trainer billboard shows a young man on a stage after a dance performance. His hands are still [shakeing|shaking|Drop the e before -ing: shake becomes 'shaking'.], and he is not looking at the audience. Instead, he watches the younger dancer who has [came|come|After 'has', use the past participle: come.] up beside him. Their trainers match but their clothes [does|do|'Their clothes' is plural, so use 'do not'.] not. The line “The next step is yours” runs between them. The designer logo is large, while the release date and stockists [appears|appear|'The release date and stockists' is plural, so use 'appear'.] in small text.

title: Waterproof coat
text: A waterproof-coat billboard outside a station shows two grandparents and their grandson walking through heavy rain. The child [splashs|splashes|Add -es after sh: splashes.] ahead while the adults [carries|carry|'The adults' is plural, so use 'carry'.] shopping bags. All three wear the same coat in different [size|sizes|After 'different', use a plural noun: sizes.]. A close inset shows water running off a sleeve. The line “The weather doesn’t choose your age” appears above a price range. The muddy path and wet shopping bags [makes|make|'The path and the bags' is plural, so use 'make'.] the scene look like an ordinary trip home.

title: Designer coat
text: Before a cinema film, a designer-coat advert opens with a tailor drawing a pattern in a quiet workshop. An older male model [trys|tries|Change y to -ies: tries.] the finished coat, then passes a mirror to a younger woman wearing a version of the same design. Both [looks|look|'Both' is plural, so use 'look'.] at their own [reflection's|reflections|This is a plural, not belonging, so it has no apostrophe: reflections.] rather than each other. Piano music plays as the camera moves over the stitching. The brand name and the words “Made to be kept” [appears|appear|'The brand name and the words' is plural, so use 'appear'.] without a price.

title: Basic handbag
text: A television advert follows a young care worker carrying a basic handbag between three homes. She takes out keys, a notebook and a birthday card for one of the people she [visit|visits|'She' takes a verb with -s: visits.]. At the end of the day she [place|places|'She' takes a verb with -s: places.] the bag beside her own kitchen table. A voiceover calls it “a place for everything you carry.” The price appears clearly on screen, while the people she helps [is|are|'The people' is plural, so use 'are'.] shown speaking with her rather than waiting [silent|silently|Use the adverb 'silently' to say how they might wait.].

title: Designer handbag
text: In a radio advert for a designer handbag, a woman describes finding her [mothers|mother’s|Add ’s to show that the bag belonged to her mother.] old bag at the back of a cupboard. The leather has marks from use, but she remembers [carried|carrying|After 'remembers', use the -ing form for a memory: remembers carrying.] it to her first job interview. A second voice explains that the brand [repair|repairs|'The brand' is singular, so add -s.] older pieces. We hear the clasp click shut. The advert ends with the name of the repair service and an invitation to make a private [appointement|appointment|Spell 'appointment' as appoint + ment.].

title: Everyday fragrance
text: An online video for an everyday fragrance shows a boy preparing for a school dance. He tries several shirts, [choose|chooses|'He' takes a verb with -s: chooses.] the one he already owns and uses a [few|little|Use 'a little' with uncountable nouns like fragrance.] fragrance before leaving. At the dance, he spends more time helping a nervous friend [then|than|'Then' is about time. Use 'than' to compare.] trying to impress anyone. The final screen says, “Feel like yourself,” beside the bottle and its price. The music is light and the party looks small enough to feel familiar.

title: Luxury perfume
text: Before a film, a luxury-perfume advert follows a woman through an empty museum after closing. She stops before a painting of a person [who's|whose|'Who's' means 'who is'. 'Whose' shows belonging: whose face.] face is turned away, then takes a small bottle from her bag. The scent is never [describe|described|After 'is never', use the past participle: described.]. Deep blue lighting and slow strings [shapes|shape|'Lighting and strings' is plural, so use 'shape'.] the mood. The brand name appears over the painting at the end, with the words “Leave something unseen.” There is no price or [informations|information|'Information' is uncountable, so it has no plural.] about ingredients.

title: Budget smartphone
text: A television advert shows a budget smartphone passing between three members of one family. A grandmother calls her son, he checks a recipe, and his daughter [use|uses|'His daughter' is one person, so add -s.] the camera for a school project. Each person [change|changes|'Each person' takes a singular verb: changes.] one setting to suit them. The phone is shown clearly rather than [hide|hidden|Match 'shown': the phone is not 'hidden'.] in their hands. The voiceover names the battery life and storage, then states the price. A final shot shows the family sitting together without [screen's|screens|This is a plural, not belonging, so it has no apostrophe: screens.].

title: Flagship smartphone
text: A banner on a photography website shows a flagship smartphone taking a picture of a musician under streetlights. A second image [display|displays|'A second image' is singular, so add -s.] the photograph in close detail, with the [musicians|musician’s|Add ’s to show that the face belongs to the musician.] face still visible. The photographer is a woman wearing a work uniform who has [stop|stopped|After 'has', use the past participle: stopped.] on her way home. The line “Keep what catches your eye” appears above a button labelled “Explore the camera.” The phone’s price [require|requires|'The phone's price' is singular, so add -s.] another click.

title: Language-learning app
text: A sponsored social post shows a teenage girl using a language-learning app before [meet|meeting|After 'before', use the -ing form: before meeting.] her [grandfathers|grandfather’s|Add ’s to show that the friends belong to her grandfather.] friends. She practises a greeting on the bus and then speaks to them at the table. One of them [correct|corrects|'One of them' is singular, so use 'corrects'.] her [gentle|gently|Use the adverb 'gently' to say how he corrects her.], and she tries again. The caption asks, “Who would you like to speak to?” A green download button and the trial length appear below. The comments include learners sharing names of people they hope to visit.

title: Gaming headphones
text: Before a cinema screening, a gaming-headphone advert starts with a team [loosing|losing|'Loose' means not tight. The verb is 'lose', so use 'losing'.] an online match because they cannot hear a warning. The screen [split|splits|'The screen' is singular, so add -s.] to show the players in different homes, including a girl who [lead|leads|'Who' refers to one girl, so use 'leads'.] the next plan. With the new headphones, each voice [are|is|'Each voice' takes a singular verb: is.] clear, and they finish the game together. The slogan says, “Hear everyone on your side.” The final shot shows the microphone, product price and shop website.

title: Premium noise-cancelling headphones
text: A radio advert for premium noise-cancelling headphones begins with crowded café sounds. A woman tells her friend she needs to finish [write|writing|After 'finish', use the -ing form: finish writing.] a song before her train [leave|leaves|'Her train' is singular, so add -s.]. After she puts on the headphones, we hear the melody she is building rather than the room. She takes them off to [answering|answer|After 'to', use the base verb: to answer.] her friend. The narrator explains that listeners can control which sounds [comes|come|'Which sounds' is plural, so use 'come'.] through, then names the model and its premium price.

title: Family tablet
text: In this television advert for a family tablet, three siblings share the screen on a rainy afternoon. One [draw|draws|'One' is singular, so use 'draws'.] a dragon, another reads aloud, and the [older|oldest|There are three siblings, so use the superlative: oldest.] helps their grandmother join a video call. Their parents appear [brief|briefly|Use the adverb 'briefly' to say how they appear.] in the kitchen but [does|do|'Their parents' is plural, so use 'do not'.] not direct every activity. A final shot shows the tablet propped up for a family recipe. The voiceover calls it “a screen for doing things together,” and the price appears beside a short warranty notice.

title: Professional camera
text: A website banner for a professional camera shows two portraits of the same street vendor. In one, he is a blurred figure behind his stall; in the other, his face and hands [is|are|'His face and hands' is plural, so use 'are'.] [sharp|sharply|Use the adverb 'sharply' before 'focused'.] focused. The photographer, a young woman, appears in a small reflection rather than the main frame. Text reads, “See the person in the picture.” A clickable panel [open|opens|'A clickable panel' is singular, so add -s.] specifications and sample images, while a caption identifies the vendor by name with his [permision|permission|Spell 'permission' with a double s.].

title: Fitness tracker
text: This podcast advert for a fitness tracker is recorded as a conversation between a runner and her father. She describes training for a race; he describes walking every evening after [recover|recovering|After 'after', use the -ing form: after recovering.] from an illness. Both [checks|check|'Both' is plural, so use 'check'.] their progress on the same device, but neither mentions losing weight. Their different goals [makes|make|'Their different goals' is plural, so use 'make'.] exercise seem possible at more than one age or level of fitness. The host gives the price and says the tracker can be [use|used|After 'can be', use the past participle: used.] without a paid coaching plan.

title: Home security system
text: In a radio advert for a home security system, a woman hears her front gate open while she is working [lately|late|'Lately' means 'recently'. After the normal time is 'late'.]. Her phone tells her that her teenage son has [arrive|arrived|After 'has', use the past participle: arrived.] home, and she asks if he [want|wants|'He' takes a verb with -s: wants.] dinner. The scene is calm rather than [frightened|frightening|The scene would cause fear, so use 'frightening'.]. A voiceover explains the camera alert and door sensor before saying, “Know when your people are home.” The advert presents security as everyday reassurance, then gives a website and a monthly subscription price.

title: Entry-level laptop
text: A website banner for an entry-level laptop is [divide|divided|After 'is', use the past participle: divided.] into three moving pictures. A student edits a school project, a mechanic checks a repair manual, and an older man writes to his sister. Each person [use|uses|'Each person' takes a singular verb: uses.] the same model in a different place. The line “Ready for your next task” appears over a [clear|clearly|Use the adverb 'clearly' before 'displayed'.] displayed starting price. When visitors tap the banner, they see the [laptops|laptop's|Add 's to show that the storage belongs to the laptop.] storage, battery life and accessibility settings rather than a picture of an expensive office.

title: Family car
text: This television advert for a family car opens with a father trying to fit a large cake into the boot. His daughter offers a [best|better|She is comparing her way with his, so use 'better'.] way to arrange the bags, while her mother checks the [root|route|A 'root' is part of a plant. The way you travel is a 'route'.] from the passenger seat. They arrive at a crowded birthday party with the cake intact. The car's space is [demonstrate|demonstrated|After 'is', use the past participle: demonstrated.] through a small problem rather than a list of numbers. A price and safety rating [appears|appear|'A price and safety rating' is plural, so use 'appear'.] on screen after the family goes inside.

title: Luxury car
text: A luxury car advert on television follows a woman driving through a city before dawn. She stops to collect her elderly father, who [quiet|quietly|Use the adverb 'quietly' to say how he admires it.] admires the [comfortible|comfortable|Spell 'comfortable' with -able.] seat. No one mistakes her for a chauffeur or [congratulate|congratulates|'No one' takes a singular verb: congratulates.] her for [own|owning|After 'for', use the -ing form: for owning.] the car. The camera lingers on the interior, then widens to show a busy morning street. “Make room for what matters,” says the voiceover. The brand name appears at the end, with no price or finance offer.

title: City bicycle
text: A sponsored social post for a city bicycle follows a nurse leaving work at sunset. She rides along a marked cycle lane, stops for [grocerys|groceries|Change y to -ies: groceries.] and [reach|reaches|'She' takes a verb with -s: reaches.] home before the rain. The caption says, “A different way across town,” and lists the [bikes|bike's|Add 's to show that the lights belong to the bike.] lights and carrying basket. The nurse is shown as [tiring|tired|The nurse feels the tiredness, so use 'tired'.] but capable, and the city has ordinary traffic rather than empty streets. A second image gives the price, sizing guide and nearby shops.

title: Racing bicycle
text: In a social post for a racing bicycle, a cyclist finishes a difficult climb and [wait|waits|'A cyclist' is one person, so add -s.] at the top for the rest of her club. The photos include riders of different ages, though the lightest and most expensive bike is [her's|hers|'Hers' never has an apostrophe.]. The caption describes the [frames|frame's|Add 's to show that the weight belongs to the frame.] weight and a race result, then invites readers to explore the specifications. The group photograph keeps the focus on shared training instead of presenting success as something [achieve|achieved|Use the past participle after 'something': something achieved alone.] entirely alone.

title: Budget hotel stay
text: A podcast advert for a budget hotel stay begins with the sound of keys, [luggages|luggage|'Luggage' is uncountable, so it has no plural.] wheels and a kettle. Two friends describe returning from a concert and [make|making|Keep the list parallel: returning ... and making.] tea in their clean, small room. They joke about the view of a car park but [praises|praise|'They' is plural, so use 'praise'.] the late check-in and helpful receptionist. A narrator gives the nightly price and booking conditions. The advert treats an affordable trip as enjoyable without pretending that the room is [luxury|luxurious|After 'is', use the adjective: luxurious.].

title: Luxury hotel stay
text: This magazine advert for a luxury hotel shows a woman reading on a shaded balcony above the sea. Through the open door, a staff member [place|places|'A staff member' is one person, so add -s.] flowers on a table, but their face is not visible. The headline says, “Everything taken care of.” Gold lettering and a full-page photograph [creates|create|'Gold lettering and a photograph' is plural, so use 'create'.] a calm, expensive mood. A small note mentions private transfers and a [personnel|personal|'Personnel' means the staff of a company. 'Personal' means for one person.] host. The picture suggests comfort, while giving almost no attention to the people who [provides|provide|'Who' refers to 'the people', which is plural, so use 'provide'.] it.

title: Household vacuum cleaner
text: A social post for a household vacuum cleaner begins with a father [droping|dropping|Double the p: dropping.] a bowl of cereal just before guests arrive. His daughter fetches the vacuum and shows him which attachment [reach|reaches|'Which attachment' is singular, so add -s.] the corners. Both [laughs|laugh|'Both' is plural, so use 'laugh'.] as they clean. The caption lists the price and the machine's weight, with a link to a short demonstration. The advert presents housework as a shared family task and gives the child practical [knowledges|knowledge|'Knowledge' is uncountable, so it has no plural.] rather than making her a helpless onlooker.

title: Premium robot vacuum
text: In a magazine advert for a premium robot vacuum, an architect comes home to a tidy apartment and puts her feet up with a book. The device [cross|crosses|'The device' is singular, so add -s.] the floor in the lower corner of the picture. Text says, “One less job on your list,” and a diagram shows how it [avoid|avoids|'It' takes a verb with -s: avoids.] furniture. Her home is spacious and almost empty, making the product seem [effortlessly|effortless|After 'seem', use an adjective: effortless.] to use. The small print gives a high price and notes that some features [needs|need|'Some features' is plural, so use 'need'.] an app.

title: Flat-pack sofa
text: A website banner for a flat-pack sofa shows a family carrying three boxes up a narrow staircase. In the next moving image, two adults and a teenager [fits|fit|'Two adults and a teenager' is plural, so use 'fit'.] the pieces together while a younger child [sort|sorts|'A younger child' is one person, so add -s.] the screws. The line “Bring it home yourself” sits above a price and a link to assembly instructions. The room is a modest [renting|rented|The family rents the flat, so use 'rented' to describe it.] flat, with books on the floor. The advert makes limited space part of the story instead of [hide|hiding|After 'instead of', use the -ing form: instead of hiding.] it.

title: Designer sofa
text: In a podcast advert for a designer sofa, an interior designer describes visiting an older couple whose living room has [holded|held|The past participle of 'hold' is 'held'.] decades of family [gathering's|gatherings|This is a plural, not belonging, so it has no apostrophe: gatherings.]. They choose a new sofa together, discussing the fabric and seat height as [careful|carefully|Use the adverb 'carefully' to say how they discuss it.] as its appearance. Soft conversation and a closing door [creates|create|'Soft conversation and a closing door' is plural, so use 'create'.] the scene through sound. The host names the collection and offers a consultation link, but gives no price. The couple are presented as people with taste, not as grandparents waiting in the background.

title: Shampoo
text: A cinema advert for shampoo opens on a huge close-up of wet hair, then pulls back to [revealing|reveal|After 'to', use the base verb: to reveal.] a teenager preparing for a school concert. Her friend, who has short hair, helps her fix the microphone rather than commenting on her [appearence|appearance|Spell 'appearance' with -ance.]. As the band begins, the soundtrack grows louder and the product name appears beside a simple claim about [gently|gentle|Before a noun, use an adjective: gentle washing.] washing. The story links confidence to [perform|performing|After the preposition 'to', use the -ing form here: links confidence to performing.] with friends; the shampoo remains a small part of getting ready.

title: Premium skincare serum
text: An online video for a premium skincare serum follows a woman in her fifties through a morning at her pottery studio. She washes clay from her hands, [applys|applies|Change y to -ies: applies.] the serum and returns to her wheel. The camera shows the [line's|lines|This is a plural, not belonging, so it has no apostrophe: lines.] around her eyes [clear|clearly|Use the adverb 'clearly' to say how the camera shows them.], without a before-and-after comparison. A caption explains the ingredients and their stated purpose, while a link gives the price. She is represented through her craft as well as her skin, and her age is neither hidden [or|nor|We say 'neither ... nor'.] treated as a problem.

title: Mobile data plan
text: A podcast advert for a mobile data plan uses short voice messages between three relatives. A teenager sends a photograph from a school trip, her uncle [replys|replies|Change y to -ies: replies.] from a train, and their grandmother records a message from home. The narrator explains the shared-data allowance and what [happen|happens|'What' takes a singular verb here: what happens.] when it runs out. The voices [makes|make|'The voices' is plural, so use 'make'.] the plan seem useful across generations, while the clear limit and monthly price keep the offer understandable. The grandmother contributes the [funnyest|funniest|Change y to i: funniest.] line in the exchange.

title: Private tutoring service
text: A transit poster for a private tutoring service shows a boy and his tutor working through a maths problem at a kitchen table. The boy has [cross|crossed|After 'has', use the past participle: crossed.] out several answers, and the tutor points to one useful step rather than completing the work for him. The headline reads, “Confidence grows with practice.” A QR code [lead|leads|'A QR code' is singular, so add -s.] to tutor profiles and prices. His school uniform and neat home [suggests|suggest|'His school uniform and neat home' is plural, so use 'suggest'.] a [particuler|particular|Spell 'particular' with -ar.] kind of family, even though the wording promises help for any learner.

title: Gym membership
text: This transit poster for a gym membership shows three members [leave|leaving|After 'shows three members', use the -ing form: leaving.] a class together: a young man carrying a sports bag, a middle-aged woman using a walking stick, and an older man in running shoes. “Start where you are,” says the headline. The poster gives opening hours, [a|an|Use 'an' before a vowel sound: an introductory price.] introductory price and a map of the nearest branch. None of the people has a dramatic transformation photograph. Their different bodies [makes|make|'Their different bodies' is plural, so use 'make'.] participation the main promise rather than a particular shape.

title: Wellness retreat
text: In an online video for a wellness retreat, a teacher arrives looking [exhausting|exhausted|She feels tired, so use 'exhausted'.] and switches off her phone. Over three days she walks, joins a group meal and [spend|spends|'She' takes a verb with -s: spends.] time alone by a lake. The voiceover offers “space to think” instead of [promise|promising|After 'instead of', use the -ing form: instead of promising.] a cure. Other guests appear briefly, but staff preparing meals and leading activities remain mostly out of frame. A final card shows the location, dates and a substantial starting price, making the invitation [clear|clearly|Use the adverb 'clearly' before 'exclusive'.] exclusive.

title: Children’s board game
text: A magazine advert for a children's board game shows two cousins and their grandfather arguing [cheerful|cheerfully|Use the adverb 'cheerfully' to say how they argue.] over the rules. The youngest child notices a move that everyone else [miss|missed|Everyone missed it before she noticed, so use 'missed'.]. Colourful pieces cover the table, and the headline says, “Everyone gets a turn to surprise you.” A short box explains the age range and playing time. The photograph presents the grandfather as a player who can [loose|lose|'Loose' means not tight. To not win is to 'lose'.], while the children are shown thinking rather than [mere|merely|Use the adverb 'merely' before 'smiling'.] smiling for adults.

title: Collectable toy set
text: A transit poster for a collectable toy set places three detailed figures against a dramatic night sky. One [wear|wears|'One' is singular, so use 'wears'.] a cape, another has mechanical wings, and the third uses a wheelchair [build|built|Use the past participle to describe the wheelchair: built into a vehicle.] into a futuristic vehicle. “Build your own team” appears above a QR code linking to the full range. The small text gives the price and says the figures are sold [seperately|separately|Spell 'separately' with 'par' in the middle: se-par-ate-ly.]. The characters are presented as equally capable, although completing the advertised scene would cost [considerable|considerably|Use the adverb 'considerably' before 'more'.] more.

title: Streaming subscription
text: A website banner for a streaming subscription changes as the visitor moves over it. A grandmother watches a mystery, two teenagers [chooses|choose|'Two teenagers' is plural, so use 'choose'.] a comedy, and a young man watches a cooking programme with subtitles. The line “Find your next story” remains in the centre. A button opens the catalogue and a [clear|clearly|Use the adverb 'clearly' before 'stated'.] stated monthly price. The different viewers [suggests|suggest|'The different viewers' is plural, so use 'suggest'.] a broad audience, while the small print explains that some live events [requires|require|'Some live events' is plural, so use 'require'.] an additional payment.

title: Premium bank account
text: This magazine advert for a premium bank account shows a woman standing at an airport window, looking over a city at night. Her suitcase and business papers [suggests|suggest|'Her suitcase and business papers' is plural, so use 'suggest'.] frequent travel, but the advert never states her job. The headline reads, “Wherever work takes you.” A smaller panel lists travel support, lounge access and the monthly fee. The image presents her as [independant|independent|Spell 'independent' with -ent.] and successful, while the benefits and setting [infer|imply|Readers 'infer'. The advert 'implies'.] that this version of success [require|requires|'This version of success' is singular, so add -s.] considerable income.

title: Orange juice
text: Before a cinema screening, an orange juice advert fills the screen with a family kitchen at dawn. A grandfather cuts fruit while his granddaughter prepares breakfast for everyone else; the parents [hurries|hurry|'The parents' is plural, so use 'hurry'.] in from their night shifts. As the juice is [pored|poured|To 'pore over' something is to study it closely. Liquid is 'poured'.], the pale room turns warm and bright. The line “Start together, whenever your day begins” [acknowledge|acknowledges|'The line' is singular, so add -s.] that not every family keeps conventional hours. The carton and a promotional price appear only at the end, alongside small print about [it's|its|'It's' means 'it is'. 'Its' shows belonging: its sugar content.] sugar content. No single parent is [assign|assigned|After 'is', use the past participle for the passive: is assigned.] the task of feeding the household.

title: Cold-pressed juice
text: A website banner for cold-pressed juice shows a chef finishing work in a spotless restaurant kitchen. She opens a glass bottle and takes a break beside another chef, [who's|whose|'Who's' means 'who is'. 'Whose' shows belonging: whose apron.] apron is stained from service. A moving close-up highlights the liquid's colour and the ingredients [listing|listed|The ingredients are listed on the label, so use the past participle.] on its label. The line “Made for the hours you put in” connects an expensive drink with professional effort rather [then|than|We say 'rather than'.] effortless wellness. A button reveals the price and delivery area. The kitchen workers have names in the caption, although the cleaners who appear in the background [does|do|'The cleaners' is plural, so use 'do not'.] not.

title: Breakfast cereal
text: This transit poster for breakfast cereal depicts a father and son waiting for an early bus, each holding a bowl with a secure lid. Their school and work bags [sits|sit|'Their school and work bags' is plural, so use 'sit'.] between them. A small drawing explains the [cereals|cereal's|Add 's to show that the ingredients belong to the cereal.] wholegrain ingredients, while the headline says, “Breakfast travels with you.” The boy is pointing out a bird on the pavement; his father listens rather than staring at his phone. The poster treats their journey as [ordinarily|ordinary|Before a noun phrase, use the adjective: ordinary family time.] family time. The colourful packaging and a supermarket price [occupies|occupy|'The packaging and a price' is plural, so use 'occupy'.] the lower corner, where commuters can read [it|them|'Them' refers to the packaging and the price, which are plural.] quickly.

title: Boxed chocolates
text: In a magazine advert for boxed chocolates, an older woman opens the door to find her adult daughter standing [their|there|'Their' shows belonging. A place is 'there'.] unexpectedly. They share the chocolates over tea while a family photograph [remain|remains|'A family photograph' is singular, so add -s.] partly visible behind them. The photograph and warm indoor light [suggests|suggest|'The photograph and warm indoor light' is plural, so use 'suggest'.] a long relationship without explaining why the daughter has returned. “Some visits deserve a proper pause” appears beneath the box. The image presents the gift as a way to begin a conversation, not a replacement for one. The premium price is absent, [despite|although|'Despite' is followed by a noun or an -ing form. Before a clause, use 'although'.] the shop address and handmade claim are printed below.

title: Instant noodles
text: A cinema advert for instant noodles begins with the imposing soundtrack of an action film. A student [stride|strides|'A student' is singular, so add -s.] through a dark corridor towards a glowing kitchen, only for the camera to reveal that her dramatic mission is to prepare a late [super|supper|'Super' means excellent. An evening meal is 'supper'.]. Her flatmate joins her, and the heroic music gives way to their laughter. A close-up shows the packet, cooking time and price. The joke gives both young [woman|women|After 'both', use the plural: women.] control of the story rather than using them as decoration. The final slogan, “Big night, small budget,” makes the ordinary meal [feels|feel|After 'makes the meal', use the base verb: feel.] playful.

title: Meal kit
text: A radio advert for a meal kit plays the sound of a front door opening, followed by a quick exchange between two housemates. One has [brang|brought|The past participle of 'bring' is 'brought'.] home the ingredients; the other reads the instructions aloud and admits that he has never cooked the dish. We hear chopping, a small mistake and finally plates being [sat|set|'Sat' comes from 'sit'. Plates are 'set' down.] down. A narrator explains the subscription price and how to skip a week. Their conversation makes cooking [sounds|sound|After 'makes cooking', use the base verb: sound.] learnable and shared, while the [absense|absence|Spell 'absence' with -ence.] of an expert chef avoids [suggest|suggesting|After 'avoid', use the -ing form: avoids suggesting.] that only confident cooks can use the service.

title: Supermarket coffee
text: This television advert for supermarket coffee follows a city bus driver through a winter morning. At the depot, she pours coffee into a flask and offers another cup to a colleague [which|who|Use 'who' for a person.] has just finished his shift. Outside, the city [slow|slowly|Use the adverb 'slowly' to say how the city wakes.] wakes. The brand appears on the familiar supermarket packet beside a modest price. “For the starts nobody sees” is [spoke|spoken|After 'is', use the past participle: spoken.] over a shot of the driver greeting her first passengers. The advert gives dignity to routine work, although its warm portrait of early shifts leaves [few|little|Use 'little' with uncountable nouns like room.] room for their physical strain.

title: Speciality coffee
text: A billboard for speciality coffee shows two farmers standing beside coffee plants after rain. Their names and the region [appears|appear|'Their names and the region' is plural, so use 'appear'.] in large type, while the [roasters|roaster's|Add 's to show that the brand belongs to the roaster.] brand is smaller. The line “Know whose morning begins yours” sits above a drawing of the [bean's|beans'|Many beans are meant, so the apostrophe goes after the s: beans'.] journey to the café. At street level, a QR code links to a longer account and the premium price. The image gives the growers a visible identity, but the single photograph cannot show how the price is [devided|divided|Spell 'divided' with di- at the start.] among everyone [involving|involved|Use the past participle after 'everyone': everyone involved.] in production.

title: Sports drink
text: On a billboard for a sports drink, a teenage goalkeeper has just made a save in a muddy local match. Teammates [runs|run|'Teammates' is plural, so use 'run'.] towards her, while a boy on the opposing side gets up and smiles [although|despite|Before a noun phrase like 'the missed goal', use 'despite'.] the missed goal. The slogan, “Ready for the next minute,” is printed beside the bottle. Rather than using a stadium or celebrity athlete, the advert places sporting [achievment|achievement|Spell 'achievement' as achieve + ment.] on an ordinary public pitch. A small nutrition panel sits at the bottom, but drivers passing quickly may notice the triumphant image long before the [drinks|drink's|Add 's to show that the ingredients belong to the drink.] ingredients.

title: Bottled water
text: A radio advert for bottled water opens with the sounds of a crowded train and a child asking for a drink. Her father offers a refillable bottle, then [notice|notices|'Her father' is one person, so add -s.] that it is empty. At the next stop they buy water, and he promises to refill the bottle when they get home. The narrator gives the price and describes the [caps|cap's|Add 's to show that the material belongs to the cap.] recycled material. This small, [slight|slightly|Use the adverb 'slightly' before an adjective.] awkward story presents bottled water as useful on occasion rather than an essential daily purchase. The child is [aloud|allowed|'Aloud' means so that others can hear. 'Allowed' means permitted.] to question her father's forgetfulness.

title: Everyday watch
text: In this radio advert for an everyday watch, a man misses the time because his phone battery has [dyed|died|To 'dye' something is to colour it. A battery that stops working has 'died'.] during a school sports day. His daughter, who is competing, calls out the minutes before her race [begin|begins|'Her race' is singular, so add -s.]. Later, he fastens a simple watch around his wrist. The ticking sound becomes part of the closing music, followed by a clear price and shop name. The story presents fatherhood through attention and [reliable|reliability|After 'and', match the noun 'attention' with a noun: reliability.], while the daughter remains the athlete [who's|whose|'Who's' means 'who is'. 'Whose' shows belonging: whose event.] event gives the watch its meaning.

title: Luxury watch
text: A cinema advert for a luxury watch shows a female conductor preparing an orchestra. The auditorium is empty as she [rises|raises|'Rise' has no object. She 'raises' her hand.] her hand, and a close-up reveals the watch beneath her sleeve. Sound [drop|drops|'Sound' takes a singular verb: drops.] away for a second before the musicians begin together. “Time belongs to the person who makes the moment” appears against black. The campaign gives an older woman authority and professional skill, rather than showing her as someone's partner. The instrument makers and musicians [remains|remain|'The instrument makers and musicians' is plural, so use 'remain'.] mostly anonymous, while the final gold logo and absence of a price [signals|signal|'The logo and absence of a price' is plural, so use 'signal'.] exclusivity.

title: School trainers
text: A sponsored social post for school trainers features four pupils preparing for different parts of their day: a walk to school, a basketball game, a dance rehearsal and the journey home. A carousel [let|lets|'A carousel' is singular, so add -s.] viewers swipe between worn [souls|soles|A 'soul' is a person's spirit. The bottom of a shoe is the 'sole'.] and clean new shoes. The caption gives a price, available sizes and a link to a repair scheme. Each child [name|names|'Each child' takes a singular verb: names.] something they enjoy doing, so the shoes [supports|support|'The shoes' is plural, so use 'support'.] distinct personalities rather than creating one ideal kind of pupil. A visible “Ad” label sits above the first photograph.

title: Designer trainers
text: A website banner for designer trainers presents a young violinist walking across a city in formal concert clothes and [bright|brightly|Use the adverb 'brightly' before 'coloured'.] coloured shoes. As she moves, the banner briefly [freeze|freezes|'The banner' is singular, so add -s.] on details of the stitching and sole. The headline reads, “No uniform for ambition.” A link opens an interview about her work, followed by product photographs and a high price. Her skill offers a more specific identity [then|than|'Then' is about time. Use 'than' to compare.] the usual street-style pose, although the expensive shoes are framed as an expression of [independance|independence|Spell 'independence' with -ence.] that many viewers cannot afford.

title: Waterproof coat
text: A website banner for a waterproof coat shows a woman and her teenage nephew waiting at a rainy football pitch. She [coach|coaches|'She' takes a verb with -s: coaches.] his team, and he holds her clipboard while she demonstrates [were|where|'Were' is a verb. 'Where' introduces a place.] the players should stand. Raindrops [runs|run|'Raindrops' is plural, so use 'run'.] off her coat beneath the words “Stay for the whole game.” A clickable lower strip reveals the price, size range and waterproof rating. The advert avoids presenting outdoor activity as a test of toughness; the coach is there for the [childrens|children|'Children' is already plural.], and the coat makes staying comfortable possible.

title: Designer coat
text: In a sponsored social post for a designer coat, an architect stands on an unfinished [buildings|building's|Add 's to show that the roof belongs to the building.] roof, examining her drawings against the skyline. The long coat moves in the wind, contrasting [from|with|We say 'contrast with' something.] the practical boots beneath it. The caption names the design house and describes the fabric, while the “Ad” label and shop link [is|are|'The label and shop link' is plural, so use 'are'.] clearly visible. She is represented as someone whose decisions [shapes|shape|'Whose decisions' is plural, so use 'shape'.] the city, though the campaign uses her workplace mainly as a striking background. Construction workers appear in one wide shot without being [name|named|After 'being', use the past participle: being named.].

title: Basic handbag
text: A cinema advert for a basic handbag follows a mother teaching her son to [travelling|travel|After 'teach someone to', use the base verb: to travel.] across town alone. She packs a map, snacks and her own keys into a sturdy bag, then lets him carry his ticket and [chose|choose|After 'lets him', both verbs are in the base form: carry and choose.] the right bus. When they reach his destination, he walks ahead [confident|confidently|Use the adverb 'confidently' to say how he walks.]. The bag's compartments are shown through the action, and the final card gives a price. The story recognises the mother's care but also shows her gradually handing [responsability|responsibility|Spell 'responsibility' with -ibility.] to the child rather than holding him back.

title: Designer handbag
text: In an online video for a designer handbag, a young museum curator prepares an exhibition opening. She carries handwritten notes and a small repair kit in the bag as she checks the display. Guests arrive, and the camera shifts from her [anxiously|anxious|Before a noun, use an adjective: her anxious expression.] expression to the work she has [organise|organised|After 'has', use the past participle: organised.]. The caption links to the handbag and lists [it's|its|'It's' means 'it is'. 'Its' shows belonging: its materials.] materials without showing a price until the viewer clicks. The advert presents professional achievement as attractive, yet its close-ups repeatedly [returns|return|'Its close-ups' is plural, so use 'return'.] from the exhibition to the expensive object on her arm.

title: Everyday fragrance
text: This television advert for everyday fragrance follows [an|a|Use 'a' before a 'you' sound: a university.] university student visiting his grandmother before an important interview. She recognises the scent and tells him that his grandfather [use|used|We say 'used to' for past habits.] to wear something similar, then helps him straighten his collar. In the next scene he enters the interview room, where a woman [lead|leads|'A woman' is singular, so add -s.] the panel. The slogan reads, “A little courage goes with you.” Packaging and a supermarket price close the advert. The fragrance is tied to memory and reassurance rather than a promise that wearing it will [garantee|guarantee|Spell 'guarantee' with gua-.] success.

title: Luxury perfume
text: A radio advert for luxury perfume begins with a woman describing an empty theatre from the stage. We hear her footsteps, a curtain moving and the distant sound of an audience arriving. She says the scent [remind|reminds|'The scent' is singular, so add -s.] her of the first performance she directed, when she finally [trusts|trusted|This happened in the past, so use 'trusted'.] her own decisions. A low voice names the perfume and a department store, but [offer|offers|'A low voice' is singular, so add -s.] no ingredients or price. The advert gives her a creative history; listeners must imagine both her appearance and the expensive bottle being [sell|sold|After 'being', use the past participle: being sold.].

title: Budget smartphone
text: This transit poster for a budget smartphone shows a cleaner calling her daughter after an evening shift. The daughter is sitting at a desk with a map of the city, helping plan [tomorrows|tomorrow's|Add 's to show that the route belongs to tomorrow.] route. The headline promises “The conversations that matter, at a price that works.” A large figure gives the phone's starting cost, with storage and contract details underneath. The mother is represented as an active parent [manage|managing|Use the -ing form to describe the parent: a parent managing time.] time and money. The poster's emotional scene is [support|supported|After 'is', use the past participle for the passive: is supported.] by [practicle|practical|Spell 'practical' with -al.] information that passing commuters can check.

title: Flagship smartphone
text: In a television advert for a flagship smartphone, a young documentary maker films her [neighbourhoods|neighbourhood's|Add 's to show that the festival belongs to the neighbourhood.] annual street festival. She records a drummer, an older baker and children making decorations, then shows the finished short film at an outdoor gathering. Fast cuts [demonstrates|demonstrate|'Fast cuts' is plural, so use 'demonstrate'.] the camera's low-light performance, while a title card names the feature. “Every place has a story worth keeping” closes the advert. The expensive handset is associated [to|with|We say 'associated with' something.] a community's visibility, although the story depends [of|on|We say 'depend on' something.] one person owning the latest technology.

title: Language-learning app
text: A billboard for a language-learning app depicts a woman ordering food in two overlapping photographs. In the first she [point|points|'She' takes a verb with -s: points.] at the menu, while in the second she laughs with the waiter and speaks a short sentence [print|printed|Use the past participle to describe the sentence: printed in a speech bubble.] in a speech bubble. The headline asks, “What could you say next month?” A QR code offers a trial and a line below [explain|explains|'A line' is singular, so add -s.] the subscription price afterwards. The woman is neither mocked for making mistakes [or|nor|We say 'neither ... nor'.] transformed into a perfect speaker; the change is presented as increased willingness to try.

title: Gaming headphones
text: Before a cinema screening, an advert for gaming headphones opens with a player hearing a [teammates|teammate's|Add 's to show that the warning belongs to a teammate.] quiet warning behind the film's booming soundtrack. A split screen shows four friends in separate rooms, including a boy using a wheelchair who [direct|directs|'Who' refers to one boy, so use 'directs'.] their strategy. Their voices [becomes|become|'Their voices' is plural, so use 'become'.] clearer as the game unfolds, and the final victory is collective.
